content: The use of ipecac syrup is no longer recommended for poisonings. Activated charcoal is now the preferred treatment. For adults, administer 15-30 mL of activated charcoal orally once. If vomiting does not occur within 20-30 minutes, a second dose of 15 mL may be given. If vomiting still does not occur within 30-45 minutes after the second dose, gastric lavage should be performed. Administer the dose with 3-4 glasses of water. For children under 6-12 months of age, administer 5-10 mL of activated charcoal orally once with 4-8 ounces of water, but only under medical supervision. For children aged 1-12 years, administer 15 mL orally once with 1-2 glasses of water. A second dose of 15 mL may be given if vomiting does not occur within 20-30 minutes. For individuals over 12 years of age, the dosing is the same as for adults: 15-30 mL orally once with 3-4 glasses of water, with the option to repeat a 15 mL dose if vomiting does not occur within 20-30 minutes. If vomiting does not occur within 30-45 minutes after the second dose, gastric lavage should be performed. Prolonged vomiting, aspiration, central nervous system (CNS) depression, Mallory-Weiss tears, and delays in other therapies (such as activated charcoal or N-acetylcysteine) are potential complications. Vomiting-induced vagal bradycardia, lethargy, absent gag reflex, and coma are also possible adverse effects. The short time between poison ingestion and the administration of charcoal or lavage is critical. A history of ingesting substances that cause CNS depression or seizures, as well as the ingestion of caustics, volatile liquids, or sharp objects, are contraindications for the use of ipecac syrup. Additionally, ipecac syrup may not be effective on an empty stomach. It is important not to confuse ipecac syrup with ipecac fluid extract, which is 14 times stronger. Ipecac syrup is not indicated if the patient has already experienced spontaneous vomiting. Its use is falling out of favor with many poison control centers, as prolonged vomiting may delay gastric lavage. The effectiveness of ipecac syrup may be reduced if taken with milk or carbonated beverages. Abuse of ipecac syrup has been reported in patients with bulimia or anorexia nervosa, and it has been associated with cardiomyopathies and death in individuals with eating disorders. If ipecac syrup is not vomited and is absorbed, it may be cardiotoxic. The absorption of emetine, one of its alkaloids, can result in heart conduction disturbances. Ipecac syrup is classified as Pregnancy Category C. It is unknown whether it is excreted in breast milk, so caution is advised during lactation. Pregnancy Category C indicates that risk to the fetus cannot be ruled out, as controlled studies in pregnant women are lacking. Ipecac syrup acts as a gastric irritant and stimulates the chemoreceptor trigger zone in the CNS through its alkaloids, emetine and cephaeline, to induce vomiting. It is most effective when administered within 30 minutes of poison ingestion. However, significant absorption of the drug can occur if emesis is not produced. The above information is provided for general informational and educational purposes only. Individual treatment plans may vary, and formulary information is subject to change. Always consult the applicable healthcare provider or poison control center for the most current and accurate information.
